utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. The Chamber also regrets that we were not in a position to start in time. Mr. Stewart, are you ready to continue cross-examination of Mr. Mandic?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Before doing so, but perhaps I don't know, Madam Usher, whether Mr. Mandic is nearby or not, but I would need approximately 90 seconds before he comes in. First of all, I'd like to draw the attention of the parties to the fact that we should finish this witness by tomorrow, by Friday, and that the Chamber would need approximately 45 minutes on Friday for procedural matters. Then, finally, may I give the following guidance to the Defence, and it's guidance by way of example. This Chamber, which is composed of professional Judges, this Chamber does understand, even without any further explanation, that a signature of a speaker of an assembly is normally the expression of the fulfilment of the professional duties of that speaker, that is, to sign texts adopted by that assembly, and is, as such, rather an expression that the speaker fulfilled his constitutional duties related to that position, rather than anything else, and certainly is not, as such, an expression of any special involvement in the creation and/or the adoption of the relevant text. This is just by way of an example. Some questions were put to the witness which really could have been saved because the Chamber understands this, even without further explanation of the witness. Perhaps it's, as I said, it's guidance by way of example. I would like to ask the Defence to keep that in mind, and I'd like to ask the usher now to escort the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, may I just say, Your Honour, we welcome that guidance, and I understand it to mean that Your Honour is inviting us to apply it by analogy to similar situations. Your Honour, we would have been more cautious before that guidance, since occasionally emphasis is laid by the Prosecution on such formal matters. But we find that guidance extremely helpful, Your Honour, and we will apply it sensibly by analogy in every available situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I take it that the Prosecution, by listening to the guidance we gave to you, also understands this to be of some importance for the Prosecution as well

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, good afternoon. Mr. Tomic, good afternoon to you as well. Mr. Mandic, may I remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony. Mr. Stewart, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, good afternoon. Mr. Mandic, earlier on in the case, in the course of your evidence, I mean, that was on Tuesday, the 23rd of November, and for everybody's reference, it's at page 83 to 85. I'm totally giving up on the continuous transcript exercise, which didn't work for any of us. You gave some evidence in relation to Mr. Krajisnik and Mr. Prstojevic, and we've already explored that in the course of this cross-examination, Mr. Mandic, and I certainly don't propose, Your Honours, to go over that again. But very specifically, you said, it's at page 85 of your evidence, that: "Mr. Krajisnik could give him", that's Mr. Prstojevic, "Instructions in terms of how he should exercise power in Ilidza." Mr. Mandic, just a single question here. You don't suggest, do you, that Mr. Krajisnik had any formal authority which enabled him to give instructions to Mr. Prstojevic as his formal superior?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, I didn't mean the formal authority, but his authority as the president of the National Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, I don't propose to go back over that ground, because apart from the formal position, the other area was, we believe, adequately covered in cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, then moving to a totally different area, then. The -- you said earlier in your evidence in this case, and this is -- the day is Monday, the 29th of November. And you -- at page 9. You were asked by

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: "Did the government make known to the Presidency its concerns about irregularities and inhumane treatment in detention facilities and camps?" And you asked for clarification, whether Mr. Tieger, the Prosecutor, was referring to the Presidency of Republika Srpska, and he confirmed he was. You said: "Yes. That was done on a daily basis." Mr. Mandic, when do you say that that process began, that the government was making known to the Presidency on a daily basis such concerns?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember when such a practice started, but it was in the course of 1992. For a certain period of time after the outbreak of armed conflicts.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: But over the early months of the armed conflict, your position, Mr. Mandic, is that the government was not in possession of significant information about irregularities and inhumane treatment in detention facilities and camps; that's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And that it was broadly -- we'll come to this a little bit later in the course of your evidence, but broadly speaking, it was sometime in or possibly shortly before August that concerns about irregularities and inhumane treatment in detention facilities came to be more openly and obviously voiced and debated, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: This is a reference to a particular -- I mean, this is a paraphrasing, I believe it is paraphrasing. I'd like some particular transcript reference, if Mr. Stewart is directing the witness's attention for a particular part of his testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The parties may ask for a literal quotation to the extent needed. Mr. Stewart, Mr. Tieger is complaining about -- that you are rephrasing the evidence in such a way that it would not -- paraphrasing the evidence in a way which would not be appropriate. You're invited to draw the attention of the witness to the specific portion of the evidence by literally quoting it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. Tieger will have to be more specific because I'm not with him on that. I don't understand. I was attempting to quote specific passages absolutely as closely as could sensibly be done, which I believe I did. And I'm -- it's simply not clear to me, Your Honour. I'd invite information as which bit I've inaccurately reflected.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No. And I appreciate the fact that on earlier occasions Mr. Stewart was directing our attention to portions of the transcript and reading from those portions of the transcript. But now he seems to be talking about the information available and the timing of that information, and I am -- I don't believe we were directed to a portion of the transcript from which that arises. I wasn't complaining about a Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond general practice. I was complaining about the most recent question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. So far as most recent question is concerned, Your Honour, I wasn't purporting -- where I had quoted specifically from the transcript, and that's in relation to the phrase "irregularities and inhumane treatment in detention facilities and camps" that appeared in my question, and I was actually reading from the transcript. And the "daily basis" was a phrase from the transcript. But when I was putting to the witness a few moments ago that his position, I think it's just disappeared off the screen, but his position was that it was -- or I was putting it to him that it was around August or just before August, I wasn't purporting to put a specific passage from the transcript to the witness at all. I was doing what one can legitimately do in cross-examination, is -- I was putting a proposition to him and inviting his agreement of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Stewart, as far as I see, the phrase where the "daily basis" comes in reads, and perhaps we should draw the attention of the witness to that portion of the evidence he gave, is when you said that -- the question then put to you was: "Did the government make known to the Presidency its concerns about irregularities and inhumane treatment in detention facilities and camps?" Then you asked: "Are you referring to the Presidency of the Republika Srpska?" And then your next answer was: "That was done on a daily basis. The communications and reports were discussed in order to overcome these problems that arose at the beginning of 1992, when the whole war chaos broke out." And then the next question was: "And we were talking about government sessions in June 1992. In June 1992, through the beginning of December 1992, who were the members of the Presidency?" So then it continued. That is the evidence your attention has been drawn to by Mr. Stewart. Mr. Stewart, if you have any questions, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I'm afraid I still don't follow. It's not my obligation, unless it's in some way obviously misleading, it's not my obligation, and I apprehend the Trial Chamber wouldn't welcome it if I always went right through the whole of every question and answer rather than stopping at what I, for the purposes of my cross-examination, fairly regard as the critical points. And Your Honour has drawn attention to the passage in which it's absolutely clear that I quoted literally, including the exchange by way of clarification between Mr. Mandic and Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the concern is simply this, and perhaps it's easier to understand what's being conveyed when you hear it rather than when you're in the course of speaking it, which is sometimes difficult. Mr. Stewart began that series of questions, if I recall correctly, something -- because he was quoting from the transcript, something along the lines of "in the course of your evidence." And then as he moved through it, as he indicated, when he came to the last question, he departed from something that the witness said during the course of his evidence and was instead moving to something else. But he -- instead of signalling to the witness that that was no longer the case, in fact I think he used the expression "and your position is," which certainly would have the risk of suggesting to the witness that that was something that was said during the course of his evidence, and that needs to be made clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The matter has been clarified at this moment. As a general rule, I gave guidance to the parties that if there's any feeling that the other party would misrepresent the evidence given and hinting to it as if it were the evidence, and I now understand that there was some confusion about what exactly was the evidence and what was the general line of the evidence. The party not happy with it may ask for literal quoting, and of course, as expected, not to do that unnecessarily. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It seems, Your Honour, with respect, it seems to have been an entirely innocent misunderstanding on both sides, if I may put it that way, in relation to that particular point. The -- excuse me, Your Honour, I had to remind myself and be sure that we didn't stop with the question, because I am quite interested in answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. What I was putting to you, Mr. Mandic, and not, to make it clear, not based on any specific item in your evidence, was that the -- just putting the proposition to you to see whether you agree with it, that, broadly speaking, it was sometime in or possibly shortly before August 1992 that concerns about irregularities and inhumane treatment in detention facilities in Republika Srpska came to be more openly and obviously voiced and debated.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, you have, and again, I'm not pointing to any specific item in the transcript, but you have referred, and I invite you to confirm, that you were yourself, in the summer of 1992 and certainly through to August, September 1992 - I beg your pardon - you were a keen proponent of the unification of the civilian and military judiciary, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On two occasions, I addressed the president of the Republic, Dr. Karadzic, in writing, to speak his mind on this proposal and to instruct me if he saw -- thought to start working on the unification of the civilian and military judiciaries.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And among the problems with the bifurcation of the civilian and military jurisdictions was sheer shortage of judges, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the very beginning of the establishment of Republika Srpska, that is, the passing of the constitution, the civilian and military judiciaries had been divided. And in the beginning of the war, some judges went over to the military prosecutor's office and judiciary because salaries were higher there. This was the basic reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So among other difficulties, that was -- that was hampering your ability to establish an effective civilian judiciary in Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You were -- the position is this: We can look at documents at necessary, Mr. Mandic, but I want to avoid unnecessary grinding through paper where we can. But the position was that you, in July 1992, you specifically proposed to the government that there should be unification of military and civilian judiciary, and the government, under Mr. Djeric, rejected your proposal?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe I addressed the president of the Republika Srpska, Dr. Karadzic. There is a document to prove that, I think. Mr. Tieger showed it to me. I think that I addressed the president of the Republic first.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, I'm going to accept your, with respect, if I may put it this way, I'm going to accept that element of the answer that that's how you channelled the proposal. But it is correct that the government then considered your proposal and the government, under Mr. Djeric, rejected it?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And that was at the -- you may not remember this specifically, Mr. Mandic, or perhaps you do, but at the 39th session of the government, on the 14th of July, 1992. Do you -- it's a rather detailed suggestion.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, we can show you the document, which is -- was among Mr. Treanor's exhibits, Your Honour. It was P65, tab 13 -- I'm sorry. Binder 13, tab 179. Do you have that? And it's item --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic -- thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It's item 24. Well, we see that this is headed -- it's minutes from the 39th session of the Republika Srpska government, held on the 14th of July, chaired by -- it says Mr. Beric, but we've seen that before. His Honour draw the attention. It's an obvious misprint. Mr. Djeric. And you're not present, but Mr. Radovic is attending on your behalf. Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond Item 24, which is on page 3 of the English, Proposal of the Ministry of Justice and Administration Regarding the Transfer of Functions from Military Courts to Civil Courts. You were the moving spirit of that proposal, weren't you, Mr. Mandic?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And Mr. Radovic was my deputy.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And then that item is dealt with at page 8 of the English, page 7 of the B/C/S. And it says the decision is with respect to the letter of Ministry of Justice and administration, the following was concluded: "Military justice organs are already formed, so there is no need that the authorities are shifted from them to regular courts. However, all measures should be taken so that all the organs can start functioning." And then there's a different proposal that follows. So that was the rejection of the proposal.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I see this document now for the first time in 12 years.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And then what happened after that was that you were reluctant to accept that final -- as the final decision, weren't you, Mr. Mandic?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my opinion, for the purposes of the rule of law, the judiciary had to be unified, with special department, the civilian and the military ones, in order to ensure the rule of law as soon as possible. Not only did I submit these proposals to the government, as the OTP showed to me, I -- there were two documents with which I addressed the president of the Republic, who, in the state of an imminent threat of war, he could pass decrees with the force of a law that could be submitted for verification to the parliament. However, I never received any sort of a response to these letters. This means that it took place two months and ten days after my appointment as a minister of justice.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And you were, as we have seen, you were unsuccessful in persuading the government to adopt your proposal. You didn't obtain a positive response from the president of the Republika Srpska, Dr. Karadzic. That's right so far, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: But as you have specifically indicated at page 14 of your evidence on the 29th of November in this case, you did obtain some support for your idea from Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And specifically, what Mr. Krajisnik did agree to do was to bring the matter before the Assembly?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that I received support from Mr. Krajisnik for the unification of the judiciaries at the level of Republika Srpska. In my personal contact with him. As for the submission of this proposal either to the agenda of the government or the Assembly, Mr. Krajisnik had no authority to do that. I could myself, in writing, submit these proposals to either of these two branches of government. Mr. Krajisnik gave his approval or support to my idea that I was lobbying for ever since I had been appointed minister of justice.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: But is -- I'll pause for a moment. Let us all catch up with that. Is this the position, then, Mr. Mandic: Are you saying that you -- well, effectively, you had the right to have your proposal brought up and discussed before the Assembly?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Both before the Assembly and the government, but also before the president of the Republic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So what I put to you about Mr. Krajisnik, does it come to this: That Mr. Krajisnik was at least in a positive, practical way, he -- because he was the president with functions in relation to agendas and timetables and so on for the Assembly, he was at least supportive in that position in ensuring that, within a reasonable time, your proposal was put on the agenda for an Assembly meeting?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't discuss this. Mr. Krajisnik supported my efforts through the government and the president of the Republic to have this matter discussed and adopted at the level of the government and the Assembly, as far as I remember. I was unable to place this on the agenda of the Assembly directly without the approval of the government. I was unable to circumvent the government. As an executive branch of government that gave its approval to all the draft proposals that were then forwarded into the parliamentary procedure for adoption as laws.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, you did get it onto the agenda- I'm now coming to another document, Mr. Mandic, again from Mr. Treanor's exhibits. It's P65, and in this case it's bundle -- sorry, bundle 14. I beg your pardon. Bundle 14, tab 213. And this is -- these are -- well, it's a transcript of a tape-recording of the Republika Srpska Assembly's 22nd session, which was held in Zvornik, I have a note, on the 23rd and 24th of November, 1992. It says all that information except the Zvornik, that I've added, but it's there somewhere that it was in Zvornik. For some slightly mysterious reason, what is at page 88 of 123 in the English version is page 11 of the second part. So there's some slightly different numbering in the B/C/S. I think you perhaps just have the second part, Mr. Mandic. But towards the end there should be some lower numbering towards the -- in the second half the document, where it starts again 1 through to 11, if you have that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. Logistical issue. I'm looking at the exhibit to which counsel referred, and I see in the English, the beginning of the session at page 1 and what is clearly the conclusion of the session at page 79 of the English, at least in the -- when I refer to the tab of the particular binder that was identified. I don't know if there's an explanation for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It's --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So sorry. It's in two sections in the B/C/S, but in the English it's got a single ERN number, which is 02149632 to 02149749. And that numbering appears on every page right through to 123 of 123. So we don't stop at page 79, or whatever it was. The explanation, we seem to have been provided later, perhaps, than Mr. Treanor's evidence. This may be the explanation - with this translation. But the document that I'm looking at came to us from the Prosecution. I suppose the explanation is that perhaps it came to us after the exhibit formally was put in through Mr. Treanor. That's the best I can offer at the moment, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've found it in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. I think the problem at the moment - thank you, Mr. Mandic - is there are people in court who need to have it who haven't got it. So we're members of a restricted club here, you and I, and one or two others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It seems there's -- if it has been split up in two different portions, where some of it -- numbering continues in English, numbering restarts in the B/C/S version. That's what I -- and I think, as a matter of fact, that the B/C/S also says part 2 on the new page 1. Is it true that the first two words are "part 2" and then it continues that it's Mr. Dragan Kalinic who speaks. It seems to be --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour is right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It does say that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I mention that on page 123, what we've got now of the English, but on the last page of the second part of the B/C/S, there is a stamp, an official stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I certainly see both parts of the B/C/S to which counsel refers. If there's some simple way of resolving this at the moment, if anyone has the second -- additional copy of the second part, we can certainly move forward and take care of the -- any lingering logistics later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The second part in English or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I have -- both parts are in the binder in B/C/S, but the -- our documentation in court with -- contains --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The English version just numbers through until 123, and then it comprises both part 1 and part 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I think the problem is that Mr. Tieger's English Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond doesn't go far enough and when Mr. Hannis isn't in court, the Prosecution team have real problems with B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Does it mean your English stops at 78.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 79. Yes. Then you have a problem. The only thing, if at this moment we could have the relevant English text on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then it would certainly help us out. So this is now to be returned to the witness, the B/C/S version, and, Mr. Stewart, if you would always indicate what page we are on in English, and Madam Usher will then put that on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, of course, Your Honour, I will.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So -- well, the English doesn't -- you, Mr. Mandic, you've had the right page for ages, but for everybody else, I'm on page 88 of the English, where it says: "We have another item," and it's Mr. Krajisnik who's speaking there, of course, because he's presiding over the session. "We have another item, the proposed decision on uniting military and civilian judiciary." And then Mr. Mandic, you speak. You see that point?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I have to apologise to this Honourable Chamber, the Prosecution, and the Defence. I fail to remember that this was ever discussed before the Assembly. The only memory I have of it was through the documents that I have seen in my interviews with the Prosecutor. This document, I'm seeing it for the first time after Zvornik, and this is why I could not remember that the matter was ever discussed before the Assembly. So once again, my apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Mandic, I don't presume to speak for His Honour, but may I just say that I doubt that the Trial Chamber requires any apology for you when you don't remember. Probably only requires you to make it clear when you don't remember as the most helpful thing at all?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, is that a fair --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're right. Mr. Mandic, there's no need to apologise for not remembering something, because it's quite understandable. But please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So, Mr. Mandic, I -- again, I want to try and take it shortly here. In a nutshell, you speak, and of course you're supporting your own proposal. You point out that it would require a change in the constitution and the law. You give your reasons -- it's over the page in the English. You refer to the large number of appointments of prosecutors and judges. You say that you have a lot of problems with the matter of jurisdiction. You often don't know whether a person has been on leave, whether he's a civilian or a conscript. You're referring there to what would, under a unified system, then, be an absolutely unnecessary issue to get involved with, whether somebody is subject to civilian or military jurisdiction when they're brought before the court, and they might be brought from the wrong one. That's the problem, isn't it, that you're referring to there?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The issue concerns the subordination of courts. If there was only one judiciary, if there had been only one judiciary, there would have been fewer problems compared to the number of problems that I discussed before the Assembly in Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And you also make it clear here, don't you - it's about six lines from the bottom of the English - you say: "I think that this proposition is justified," or proposal, it would be probably in English, "I think this proposal is justified for now, but after the war they will again be separated. So you were, if I might put it this way, you were selling it to the Assembly on the basis that it was -- it was the right course in the particular circumstances during the wartime conditions, but eventually you would expect to see a more conventional division of jurisdiction?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And then we see the presiding, it is in the English translation, that's clearly Mr. Krajisnik, who then says: "If I understood correctly, we should adapt the constitution in order to be able to accept it. I think that this should be an initiative, but first we must hear the opinion of the army, then the initiative should go to our constitution commission and ministry and the headquarters or, in fact, military prosecutor and military judiciary should rewrite it for the next session. This is my suggestion." So the -- you would interpret that, Mr. Mandic, as a following wind or support from Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, as I have indicated already.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And then we see -- but public support in the Assembly, as opposed to --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: An official one.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And then General Gvero, and who exactly was he?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a member of the Main Staff. I think he was either the deputy or assistant to the Chief of Staff, Ratko Mladic. He was in charge of the internal politics within the military.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And he was -- well, you -- well, it's probably quicker if I just read it. He says: "I've asked for a word, but I wouldn't if I knew that this was only an initiative, one of these duties is on me, but I'm not a lawyer by vocation. This proposition is, in my opinion, rather strange. We should talk about what is in favour and what is against this initiative, but I think that we would act in contradiction with the constitution and the usual practice. Thank you." And then Mr. Krajisnik brings - it was a fairly short discussion there - to an end, and concludes that the initiative, or proposal, it might be called, should be given to our ministry to contact with the headquarters and discuss it with the constitution commission. He says: "After the proposition is again presented to the Assembly, we shall discuss it." So the upshot there, Mr. Mandic, was that the -- in the face of clear expression of opposition on the part of a military person, the matter was -- well, it was -- would it be fair to describe: It was pushed over to be discussed elsewhere, to be brought back on some unspecified date, if necessary, before the Assembly?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And is it correct that it never did get adopted?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Now, you were asked - and this is specifically at page 14 of the transcript of the 29th of November in this case - you were asked by

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: "Did you inform Mr. Krajisnik about the consequences or effects of the poorly functioning judiciary?" And your answer was: "I mostly consulted Mr. Krajisnik on this issue, and he helped me greatly, because he was informed about the issue of the poor functioning of the judiciary, and it seemed to me that I had his support in this idea of mine to unify the judicial system at the level of Republika Srpska." Mr. Mandic, is it possible for you to say when you first consulted Mr. Krajisnik about this particular issue?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now that my memory has been refreshed a little bit, if it was on the 27th of July that I proposed this at the session of the government, that is, July 1992, so I must have consulted Mr. Krajisnik before that. So it could have been sometime in early July, but I cannot recall the exact date. Those consultations, of course, would have been oral ones, and the debate of this proposal of mine followed. But we probably had discussed the proposal beforehand.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. In fact, Mr. Mandic, it's on the record of the documents as I put to you that the -- it happened a little bit earlier than you've just said, because the session of the government at which it rejected your proposal was itself the 14th of July. So it was at least a couple of weeks or so earlier than you've just described. But if I, just to clarify, you're saying, really, whenever you presented your proposal, you would have had some discussion with Mr. Krajisnik just before you presented it?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did you have a detailed discussion with Mr. Krajisnik about the disadvantages and effects of the divided jurisdiction or did you just summarise for him the essential problems?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The main problem was the functioning of the judiciary and the rule of law, generally speaking. All of the prisons were under the competence the military. Formally speaking, we tried to take over individual facilities, buildings belonging to the judiciary and similar. But this was not allowed by the military. My idea was to place this under one system. I did not inform Mr. Krajisnik in detail on that occasion as to what this unified judiciary would include and would be comprised of. I merely spoke to him about the situation which was very difficult and the fact that the military was somehow alienated from the rest of the system. I try to put this within the rule of law, within the system of the judiciary generally speaking, and I received full support in this regard from Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: What were the essential practical negative effects of the divided judiciary at the time that you were appointed minister of justice? Just after the middle of May 1992.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was appointed on the 19th of May. One month before that, I had been informed that I would be the minister of this civilian judiciary. At the time of my appointment, the only employees were myself, my driver, and my secretary. We didn't have any infrastructure to speak of. We didn't have any means to establish the judiciary in such a short period of time at the level of Republika Srpska. Throughout those days, I spent a lot of energy. I invested a lot of effort, together with five or six other individuals who had been employees of the judiciary from before, to establish these five courts, five district prosecutor's offices in every municipality. Now, what happened? For instance, we would appoint, within 10 to 15 days, a certain number of people to various offices, and since the salaries and the competences, generally speaking, were much better in the military, those individuals would resign and go over to the military. So that was a major problem, the problem which involved human resources. As for the organisation, the military had inherited all of the mechanisms, all of the structures, infrastructures, from the former -- from their military, both in the prosecutor's office and the judiciary. There was a lot of conflict of competences, conflict of jurisdiction, because they had competence over everything that was taking place in relation to the war, everything involving active-duty servicemen. And the majority of the male population of able-bodied men were in the military in those days. Let me give you a very banal example. A murder, a theft, or a similar offence. Until we actually went to the scene of the crime, we were not aware of who the perpetrator was and who the victim was. If one party was in the military and the other not, that would further exacerbate and complicate the situation. This led to a high level of inefficiency within the military and within the judiciary, generally speaking, and this bothered me as a professional. On several occasions, we tried to take over the correction facility in Foca from the military. We established a commission to that effect, but they simply didn't want to hand over such facilities to the judiciary, which rightfully had competence over such facilities. At the same time, we kept receiving information of a number of instances of abuse and other problems that were taking place in those facilities which were under the military at the time. The third reason for that was, financially speaking, the situation would have been much better if this unification had taken place. We would be given adequate facilities, we would have adequate human resources, and all of that put together would lead to a rule of law. And another thing that really bothered me was the behaviour of some officials from the military who were simply not adaptable enough and were not democratic enough in their mind-set. In all of this, I had the support of Mr. Krajisnik, both privately and before the Assembly, where he opposed the military on this occasion. He was a public servant with a lot of experience, and he emphasised the need to change the constitution, and he refused this at that time, and he really invested a lot of effort in trying to find the best possible solution at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You said that you referred to receiving information of a number of instances of abuse that were taking place in those facilities under the military. What sort of abuse are you referring to there?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I was referring to what was happening to the detainees who were kept in those facilities, non-Serb population.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, what was happening about which you received information?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think that they were not treated in accordance with the Geneva Conventions, I mean the people who either happened to be there at the time or were at one point brought there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And when did you first become aware yourself of such abuses?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the sessions of the government, it was the minister of the MUP, minister of the interior, who informed us thereof. I don't know when this was. I don't know the exact date. But it was in accordance with the information that was collected on the spot, in the field. People who worked in the field informed the relevant authorities of this situation, and the government at one point was able to establish that this treatment was not in accordance with both internal and international regulations. These facilities were 99 per cent under the control of the military, and only to a little extent under the control of the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You were asked, and this is at page 15 of the transcript on the 29th of November, Mr. Tieger said to you: "And is it fair to say that the poor functioning of the judiciary exacerbated the problem of trying to improve the exchange of prisoners and other detained persons or their -- or the conditions that they faced in detention facilities?" And your answer was yes. I want to just ask you about each of those, for the moment, separately. First of all, the proposition that the poor functioning of the judiciary exacerbated the problem of trying to improve the exchange of prisoners and other detained persons. In what way would a better functioning judiciary have improved the handling of the problem of exchange?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The problem of exchange was presented as a problem of the state, of the government, and that is why a commission was established at one point by the government. This commission relied on the Ministry of Justice for various professional reasons. And the unification would have led to better living conditions and better treatment of the persons who were detained in the facilities throughout Republika Srpska. These are the two elements that Mr. Tieger described as the reasons for which I requested this unification of the judiciary.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Just really wishing you to be a bit more specific, Mr. Mandic, about the, if you like, the mechanism by which a better functioning judiciary would have improved the position in relation to exchange of prisoners. What -- if you could just explain how that would have come about. What would have happened differently that then would have had the result that exchange would have gone better?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, I believed that a unified judiciary would function better in terms of the subordination between the district and municipal courts. We would dispose of more information about the people who were held, and in this way, the commissions would function better. There were representatives of the judiciary there, the MUP, the civilian authorities, and the military, and for this reason, initially we had the problem with the flow of information, because Republika Srpska was cut off into several regions. Due to the war, the flow of information from certain areas into the head office was a flawed one. In addition, the army kept everything confidential, as a military secret, which additionally aggravated the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Is it this, Mr. Mandic: That so long as the military and civilian judiciary remained separate, it enabled the military to operate more as a law unto themselves, without outside control from the civilian authorities?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is exactly what I tried to show.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And you were asked, the second limb of what you were asked by Mr. Tieger at page 15, as I cited it a few minutes ago, the proposition that the poor functioning of the judiciary exacerbated the conditions that prisoners faced in detention facilities. Was it in relation to those conditions essentially the same problem, that the military were able to operate without, in your view, effective control by civilian authorities?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Throughout my term of office as a minister, the army was entitled to control the detainees, and we're talking about more than 90 per cent of them who were held either as prisoners of war or under a different status. But it was the army who decided about them, regardless of the fact that the technical assistance in some of these facilities was provided by the civilian judiciary, that's to say, by the people employed in the civilian judiciary. The army was the organ of government which refused to adapt itself to other factors at the time, and there was nothing one could do about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And you were asked, and this is at the foot of page 21, same day, 29th of November, you were asked: "Did you tell Mr. Krajisnik what you had heard or were made aware of concerning irregularities and inhumane treatment in detention facilities and camps?" My first question there is that you making Mr. Krajisnik aware of inhumane treatment in detention camps was part of your convincing him that your proposal for the unification of the judiciary was a good idea; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, among other things.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your answer to that question, when you were asked if you did tell Mr. Krajisnik what you heard or were made aware of concerning irregularities and inhumane treatment was, and I'm quoting it from the English transcript at the top of page 22: "In general, I mostly informed Mr. Krajisnik of all the issues that I was aware of to consult with him on this particular branch of government." Mr. Mandic, do we take it that you -- it was not your job, and you didn't, in fact, report to Mr. Krajisnik in detail on some frequent basis as to what you knew?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes. There was a specific follow-up question to the series of questions to which counsel has just directed his attention on the 30th of November.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Tieger, would that not be a matter to be dealt with in re-examination, if you think that it's incomplete what Mr. Stewart draws our attention to?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, I guess my view is it's both -- it's probably more fair and perhaps more efficient as well if there's a -- if the witness's attention is directed to a particular passage and -- I know Mr. Stewart has made efforts to continue quoting the appropriate -- the passage necessary for context.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: With respect, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me say the following.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I don't mind, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, if you wouldn't mind, no problem, but usually if you stop halfway and then take out of context a certain quotation, I would agree that then the whole of the part should be read to the witness. If, however, on the next day, questions related to that would come up, it's not necessarily then -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I agree with Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. But I see Mr. Stewart seems to agree, at least --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: For this reason, Your Honour: That I don't, as a matter of fact, I don't take it and I don't believe it's intended, I don't take it as in any way an objection or criticism, because I don't expect Mr. Tieger expects me to have total mastery of what's on every day of the transcript. So if it's helpful, which it may be, for me to have this put together with some other reference on the following day, then I certainly invite that, with respect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Tieger, could you --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- same day or next day.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No. It's on the 30th and it's on page -- again, I have a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you could just allow me to open the 30th, then I -- and if instead of giving pages, if you give me one word which I could search for, then that goes quicker.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Before I move to the next intercept. This takes place immediately after the recess and when we resumed at 1.02 p.m. That's a useful guide.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, of course, has different page numbers from the --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In the sequential transcript it would be 9072. And the -- that date begins at 8996.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, the resumption at 1.02 -- search for 1.02 is on page 77.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. That's -- it seemed it must be around 76, from the --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And as you can see in the --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It's 77, Your Honour, at -- yes. I see: "Did you tell --" yes. Shall I say, I have absolutely no problem with that whatever, Your Honour, and I'll quote that passage to the witness as well, and it will be helpful to link it together.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, everybody's already got the reference and that doesn't assist you, but Mr. Tieger returned to this point and he quoted to you that question and answer, as I have just done. And then said: "I just wanted to ask you whether informing Mr. Krajisnik of all the issues included the issues of conditions in detention facilities and camps." And you said: "I will repeat what I said last time, and that is that whatever I considered or whatever I noticed regarding the government, I informed Mr. Krajisnik and asked him what to do and what should be done to overcome these problems. I most certainly informed him on the situation in Kula, because that was the only facility where I had access to in April and May of 1992. And as for the other facilities, prisons, collection centres and other facilities where prisoners of war were sheltered, or people who had undergoing ethnic cleansing and were held by the army and the police, a commission was set up to visit those camps. They submitted written reports to me and to the government on the situation there. And then through government, we would inform the Assembly and Mr. Krajisnik and all the deputies, and thereafter we would propose measures to be undertaken in order to rectify the situation. On behalf of the Presidency of the Republika Srpska, Dr. Biljana Plavsic was in charge of this particular segment, and she was involved in coordinating the issues with the International Red Cross and other international organisations in charge of these particular issues, including all the commissions from the State Commission downwards to the municipal commissions." And then you were asked: "And was the information, therefore, available to the government and available to you, as minister of justice during that time, concerning camps and allegations about conditions in camps made known to the president of the Assembly, to Mr. Krajisnik?" And you said: "Concerning all the information that I have pertaining to these particular issues, besides government, I also informed Mr. Krajisnik, and he knew about that." Now, Mr. Mandic, the first question that I have, then, arising in relation to that is -- concerns your own contacts with Mr. Krajisnik, your own direct discussions with Mr. Krajisnik. And that's not a question yet. The question is: When you were discussing yourself with Mr. Krajisnik, did you refer to irregularities and inhumane treatment in detention facilities and camps as part of your reasoning for the proposal to unify the military and civilian judiciary?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, among other things.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did you give Mr. Krajisnik, in relation to that, a broad outline of the problem of irregular and inhumane treatment, or did you go into detail about it with him?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my opinion, I did not dispose of the amount of information that he had as president of the Assembly. I would convey to him my concerns, but in broad terms. I didn't want to bother him with the details, as president of the Assembly. I just wanted to give him the totality of the problems including those in the prisons, in order to overcome them as soon as possible, because that was in accordance with our view of how these matters should be dealt with.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't know, given when we started, I don't know where -- what Your Honour prefers in relation to the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, if a suitable moment would be there now, or within the next seven or eight minutes, then -- I don't know what you still have on your mind as far as questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, I'm in the middle of a discrete topic and could carry on for five minutes or so if that were convenient to Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would that complete it or not, the next five minutes?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You never know, Your Honour, do you, because I'm only asking the questions. There's a chance, but I can't say for sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Let's see whether we can finish in the next seven minutes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Specifically, Mr. Mandic, you said, and this was page 78 on the 30th of November, you said: "I most certainly informed him," Mr. Krajisnik, "on the situation in Kula, because that was the only facility where I had access to in April and May of 1992." So you had been there yourself personally, hadn't you, Mr. Mandic?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I went there. Because, as I've already mentioned, I established the Sarajevo district and basic courts, and I had an office there that I established there when I was appointed minister. And I'm referring to a compound of buildings that were next to the prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So what specifically, so far as you remember, Mr. Mandic, which is the furthest anybody can ever go, what specifically did you then give Mr. Krajisnik by way of information about Kula?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was at Bistrica Hotel, on Jahorina. That is on the edge of the Dobrinja neighbourhood of Sarajevo. That's where there was intense fighting at the time between Serbian and Muslim forces around the Olympic Village of Dobrinja, whereby the territories controlled by the Serbs who in a way severed. On the one side, Lukavica, Pale, and Kotorac, and on the other side, Ilidza, Rajlovac, Vogosca, and other large neighbourhoods. That's where the Serb forces tried to make a corridor to connect these neighbourhoods, and the Muslim forces, on their part, tried to link up the old centre of Sarajevo with the neighbourhood of Hrasnica, Sokolovic Kolonija, and so on. For this reason, very often there were civilians who found refuge in Kula because of the fighting that took place. This was even fighting in the buildings themselves in the urban areas, and that's where I would go, and I'd inform Mr. Krajisnik about the situation there. There were cases when people in Sarajevo didn't want to accept those newcomers. There were cases of people who couldn't return to their homes because they were wrecked. And I think that even ten years later, some of these neighbourhoods and homes remain in ruins. And that's what these discussions were about. I believe it was in August that we could finally establish control over this Kula prison from the police force.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: When do you say you first informed Mr. Krajisnik about the situation in Kula?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember, but it was in early 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, early. We'd better try and be specific about "early." You had access to Kula in April and May 1992, so you're talking about after your visits there.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never came to Kula in April. I was at Vraca, as member of the MUP. It was only in May that I went up to Pale, or that's to say to Jahorina. Afterwards, it was in May/June that I started coming to the neighbourhood of Lukavica. One of the reasons for this was that at one point a decision had been taken for the government to be relocated to Ilidza. Mr. Bozidar Antic and I were tasked with finding adequate facilities to house the government, although after a certain period of time they gave up this idea. I believe this gentleman was a member of the government in charge of the economy.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So can we clarify, then, Mr. Mandic: When you said -- it's at page 78 of your evidence on the 30th of November, because I was quoting your words, you said: "I most certainly informed him, Mr. Krajisnik, on the situation in Kula, because that was the only facility where I had access to in April and May 1992." You're now saying to the Trial Chamber that actually the April was a mistake, that it was actually only in May that you personally had access to Kula?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That must have been a mistake. I was definitely at Vrace in April. I was based there with the police. You see, it is difficult to remember 12 years later whether it was the 20th of April or the 15th of May that I went to Pale. I cannot really recall at this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: We can take it, can we, then, that whatever you did report or inform Mr. Krajisnik about in relation to Kula, it was after your visit there?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I wonder -- I may have one or two more questions in this area, but in the light of the minutes that have slipped by, that may be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: -- a point for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll then have a break until 20 minutes past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Usher, please escort the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, when you informed Mr. Krajisnik of the situation in Kula, did that information include what you saw as inhumane treatment there?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never saw any inhumane treatment at Kula. As far as I knew, there was nothing inhumane that took place in Kula. My information concerning the facility at Kula, the living conditions there, the prison, the judiciary, and all, that's what I disposed of, in general terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So what was the -- if you like, what was the extremity of your concern? What were you most concerned about at Kula that you passed on to Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had never witnessed any of the members of the police who held under their control people at Kula who had either been there from before or had found shelter there from the fighting that took place in the general area. The major concern lay in the very high fluctuation of people in this prison facility and the very slow pace at which the needs of these people were provided for, like the food, clothing, and so on. But it mostly concerned the general developments and the goings-on in the Sarajevo area, including the Kula facility, that I informed Mr. Krajisnik about.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, you were asked, and the reference here is page 42 of the transcript on the 29th of November - you were asked about an exhibit which is P447. I think it's probably helpful if you do have that exhibit, 447. And what was put to you was a passage which appears on page 3 of the B/C/S version and at the very top. I'm afraid I can't help you more specifically than that, but in the English version it's at the very top. And it's the sentence that runs, and I think it's been corrected, actually, from what we see in the typed version in the English, so that it reads: "The army, crisis staffs, that is, War Presidencies." I hope I'm right in assuming that's been corrected. The army crisis staffs, that is, War Presidencies, have requested that the army round up or capture as many Muslim civilians as possible. And they leave such undefined camps to internal affairs organs. And then at the top of page 43, you said, in answer to -- it was a question by way of clarification from His Honour, Judge Orie. You said: "Your Honour, the Crisis Staff, or rather, the War Presidencies that were composed of civilians in authority requests the military and the armed forces to have as many Muslims as possible ethnically cleansed. It was not the army that requested that, but the army was requested to do that." Mr. Mandic, there is no -- you have no awareness whatever, do you, of Mr. Krajisnik being in the least bit involved in this particular request that's described, to have as many Muslims as possible rounded up or captured?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, I gave you my interpretation of this -- several lines of this paragraph, and that's in my answer concerning what the minister of the interior had written. This particular type of information was held only by the ministry that later on, through the government, forwarded to all the other bodies, this particular information.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mandic. What I was asking you about was specifically whatever did happen here. I was inviting you to confirm that you have no knowledge whatever of Mr. Krajisnik's being in any way involved in this particular request for the rounding up or capture of Muslim civilians.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Definitely not. I am certain of the fact that Mr. Krajisnik had never put forward such a request for Muslims to be rounded up or for these camps to be established.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, may I take it from this last question that you've dealt with the unification of the military and the civilian judiciary? Because I'd like to seek some clarification, some issues there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, certainly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Mandic, I'm asking you a few questions now, because it might still be fresh in your memory. You told us that Mr. Krajisnik was supporting your efforts through the government and the president of the Republic to get the unification of the civilian and military judiciary on the agenda of the Assembly, and you also explained to us that in order to get it on the agenda, you would need the approval of the government or the president.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you try to get it on the agenda just on your own? Did you make an attempt to convince those who you would have to convince to get it on the agenda first?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it is improper for me, as a minister in the government, to put an item on the agenda of the Assembly without the government's approval. It has to go through the government. As far as I remember, I was doing this with the assistance of Mr. Krajisnik, who put this item on the agenda of the Assembly, contrary to what the government or the president of the Republic wanted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Did you first ask the government to get that item on the agenda?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since the government had refused my proposal, as we could see in some of the documents here, I did not seek their approval, because the government having refused my proposal, this particular item could not be placed on the agenda of the Assembly, despite my insistence. So this was an unusual, even illegal procedure of placing the item on the agenda.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And now, how finally did you get it on the agenda? Was it Mr. Krajisnik who, upon your request, did it without informing the government, or was it that he supported you to get the approval of the government to have it put on the agenda?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe Mr. Krajisnik placed it on the agenda on my insistence, without the government's support.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I have one more. Your testimony reads as follows: "Mr. Krajisnik supported my efforts, through the government and the president of the Republic, to have this matter discussed and adopted at the level of the government and the Assembly, as far as I remember." That seems to be different from what you just answered. It at least suggests, and I understand it, but please correct me when I'm wrong, that he supported your efforts to get it on the agenda through the government or through the president. And if you'd like, I'll read it again to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I may be allowed to explain. Through personal contacts and consultations with Mr. Krajisnik, I was given his support to present this proposal for the unification of the judiciary before the government, where the proposal was rejected. He also supported my initiative to propose this in writing to the president of the Republic, which I did, but I, however, received no answer. Therefore, in respect of these two segments of the government, he unofficially provided his support, whereas when it came to the Assembly, he placed this item on the agenda to be discussed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That certainly clarifies your earlier answers. You told us that it appears from the minutes that Mr. Krajisnik opposed the military. Could you indicate where exactly you find Mr. Krajisnik opposing the military in relation to this subject.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Gvero tried to have it removed from the agenda and to leave it undiscussed entirely. As president of the Assembly, Mr. Krajisnik wanted to have the opportunity for this to be debated again between the two ministries, the Ministry of Defence and the Ministry of Justice, or rather, the Ministry of Defence and the Main Staff of the military on the one side and the Ministry of Justice on the other side. Therefore, the proposal of Gvero and these other people from the military was not accepted, that this be removed from the agenda. He gave me the opportunity to have it presented once again, that my proposal be discussed once again, despite the fact that there was resistance from the military and insistence from the military that it be removed from the agenda. This was the attitude of Mr. Gvero, and this is what his act was all about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just read to you what the words of General Gvero were, in English: "I have asked for a word, but I would not, if I knew that this was only an initiative. One of these duties is on me, but I'm not a lawyer by vocation. This proposition is, in my opinion, rather strange. We should talk about what is in favour and what is against this initiative. But I think that we would act in contradiction or decontradiction [phoen] with the constitution and the usual practice." That's what he said. You understand this to be removal of the agenda?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, to a certain extent also a mockery on the part of Mr. Gvero. If this is what he said, that this was strange and in contravention of the constitution, that he wouldn't even discuss it, although it was merely a proposal. So this was actually belittling my proposal on something that was of our common interest. It is my opinion that a proposal to have a unified judiciary could not be thought of as strange.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do understand. Were you aware that, in military circles and military judicial circles, that there was opposition against your plans?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I talked about this with General Todorovic, I believe was his name. He was the president of the supreme military court. And in my conversation with him, I didn't experience neither understanding nor rejection. However, as far as the General Staff and the people who were in charge of the military, generally speaking, are concerned, I did experience a certain amount of resistance and a lack of understanding for my idea.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for those clarifications. Please proceed, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, did General Gvero or any of the other military people concerned, did they make an attempt to have this particular item taken off the agenda before the meeting even took place?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't remember. I don't know, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You were asked, and this is page 44 of the transcript on the 29th of November, you were asked: "Was the MUP cooperating with the army in combat operations and other activities related to events in the field?" And you said that: "Yes, it was." What -- if you can say: What was the degree of cooperation that you were aware of by the MUP with army combat operations and other activities?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The MUP was subordinated to the military. In all combat activities, the military had the command over the MUP, whose members were treated as all other members of their units. This was in accordance with the constitution during the immediate threat of war, and it was also in accordance with the order issued by the president, the president of the Republic, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Could you look at or could you be given, please, Mr. Mandic, document P450, Exhibit P450. And you perhaps recall this. This is a document coming from Mr. Tomo Kovac, of the Ministry of the Interior, and addressed, and we see that, two recipients, the Serb Republic president, that was Dr. Karadzic, wasn't it, and Serb Republic prime minister, that was Mr. Djeric at this time, 8th of August, 1992. Those were the two recipients or addressees, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And this was -- just for the reference, this document was put to you and considered in your evidence as pages 49 and 55, and surrounding pages, on the 29th of November. And the second paragraph of the English says: "The basic problem in the field is that not all authorised organs are involved in the process of accommodating these people ..." that's detainees "... or in their further treatment. Therefore, there are cases where MUP members accept or in some cases even take part in capturing people in the war zones. After that, they arrange accommodation for them and a way of life. They determine the duration of their detention and their entire destiny. In another form, this is done by members of the Serb army, who are also involved in all the phases of the treatment of prisoners, similarly to the previous case." Can you say why it was that Mr. Kovac would have regarded this as a problem?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With your permission, Your Honours, the previous document of Minister Stanisic, I think, should be compared and explained in relation to this one, the Kovac document, because they are connected when it comes to the combined work of the police and the military. The document that I had in front of me a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So that's the document 447 that we were looking at a moment ago, P447. And Mr. Mandic, you're then going to offer some explanation by comparison of these two documents.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because as a former police officer and a person who knew both of these individuals, and in light of my knowledge of the problems within the police at the beginning of the war, I had professional contacts both with Tomo Kovac, while I was deputy minister, before the war, and with Mr. Stanisic. All of the problems presented by Mr. Kovac were also presented by Mr. Stanisic in the information that bears the date the 18th of July. Assistant to the police, the sixth man in the chain of importance, presented his concerns to the president of the government, to the prime minister, and this was placed on the agenda of the meeting which was chaired by the prime minister. This was somehow somewhat illogical. Also in light of the relationship between these individuals and their respective offices within the government. I had no reason to doubt the concerns of Mr. Kovac. He was to be promoted very soon, and he eventually became the minister of the interior. After 1995, that is, after the events in Srebrenica, after everything that has happened in between, now I can express certain doubts as to the concerns expressed in this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: But was the -- at least one of the specific complaints of Mr. Stanisic and Mr. Kovac that MUP members were being sucked too much into the war operations?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You were asked a number of questions by Their Honours on Wednesday, the 1st of December, that was. First, His Honour Judge Canivell asked you some questions. And at page 10 of that transcript, His Honour asked you, he said -- he asked you about the list of 57 locations. This was of prisons or detention facilities provided and about which Mrs. Plavsic explained what she felt was necessary in a television interview. And His Honour said: "You recognised that some of those places were located in Serbia, but what about the others? You knew about the existence of the others, the people that were inside?" And he -- His Honour asked you to relate that to previous questions he'd asked. You said that the list that you had seen was actually the first time you'd ever seen it. You knew there were some such camps outside Bosnia and Herzegovina, but it was Biljana Plavsic who was in charge of these matters. You said: "I was aware of some of those locations that she mentioned, but these were mostly within the Sarajevo area, the canton of Sarajevo, whereas Ms. Plavsic got her information on the other places through the military, through the MUP, or through the top leadership, and the list that we saw here yesterday or the day before yesterday was a list that I saw for the first time then." Now, in indicating sources of information that Mrs. Plavsic might have had in relation to such matters, you indicated Mrs. Plavsic's responsibilities in relation to humanitarian activities. You've already said something about that. You don't suggest, do you, Mrs. Plavsic wouldn't have got information about such matters from Mr. Krajisnik, would she?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Actually, she couldn't obtain that information from Mr. Krajisnik. She based her activities on the information that she had received from the police and the military.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And you were asked by His Honour Judge El Mahdi, you were asked a number of questions. You -- at page 19, same day, 1st of December, His Honour said: "I would like to put a question to you. Did the army depend on someone; in other words, was the army subordinated to the civilian authority, or was it working under the influence of the civilian authorities?" And you said: "No. The supreme military commander was the president of the Republic, and the chief of the General Staff was the second-ranking man issuing orders to the army. They were responsible to no one but their own institutions, from the lowest to the highest. The chief of the General Staff and the president of Republika Srpska." And then His Honour said: "And during the time that you yourself were the minister of justice, and if I'm not mistaken, you took your office in May 1992," which was obviously correct, "until the end of November 1992, could the cabinet of ministers control the army? Did they have a say in it, or what was the role of the civilian cabinet of ministers?" And you said: "At that time, there was a military justice system and the chief of the General Staff was in charge of it. He was in charge of all segments of military power and authority. The civilian authorities, even the government, were unable to make decisions contrary to the law on defence and the positions of the army and the president of the Republic. This was the case when an imminent threat of war had been declared and when all institutions were subordinate to the military." After all that, Mr. Mandic, my question is a short, simple one. It's correct, isn't it, that Mr. Krajisnik, as president of the Assembly, had no authority over the army?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And he had no other position which gave him authority over the army?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You were also asked by His Honour Judge El Mahdi -- I'm beginning with the middle of a question, which I hope His Honour will forgive me for, at the foot of page 22 of the transcript on the 1st of December.
