His Honour said: "I would like you to tell me now what sort of a relationship existed between the executive branch of the government, that is, the government itself, and the Assembly, that was the legislative branch of the government." And you answered: "At the beginning of the war, and for the most part of the first half of the war, the legislative power was wielded by the president of the Republic. Under the constitution, Article 83, I believe it was, he was entitled to pass laws himself, without the parliament, concerning all spheres of life: The army, police, justice, all the areas. The parliament had the duty to verify the law passed by the president of the state at its next session." I suggest --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Probably for the English speakers, I suggested that "ratify" is probably the word that would commonly appear in that context. At -- and you said that -- I'm sorry, you said that and then His Honour said: "Yes, but did the government answer to the Assembly for its activity?" And you said: "Yes." And His Honour said: "For instance, in this case, the government would report to the Assembly about its actions taken and activities." Now, was this the position, Mr. Mandic: That the government was certainly constitutionally under an obligation to keep the Assembly informed as to its activities, number 1?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And of course, in this -- I apologise to Their Honours if this is elementary, Mr. Mandic, but I seek your agreement. Of course the government had to act under whatever laws were passed by the Assembly or, in the particular circumstances, under the procedures as you had described them in evidence, decreed by the president of Republika Srpska. That's elementary, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: But the government was the executive organ with day-to-day responsibility for running Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the executive branch of the government, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And it was not the function of the Assembly to direct and interfere day by day with those executive functions?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're right. Mr. Stewart, sometimes when you ask me a question, and if I say "yes," I have a feeling that I will just confirm your question, or if I say "no," that it will be completely different. So can I please ask you to be a bit more specific when you phrase your questions. Because the interpretation may cause misunderstanding. "No" can turn out to be "yes," and the other way around.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, I'm aware of that problem. I think Ms. Cmeric would like to consult me on linguistic matters or allow herself to be consulted by me, perhaps; I don't know. Yes, it seems that there is exactly -- it happens in a single language, Mr. Mandic. It seems that we do occasionally run into this double-negative problem. But I believe, and Your Honours, I believe that in practice, Your Honours are not troubled by ambivalence or ambiguity as to whether the witness is agreeing with a proposition. If at any point that does happen, then if anybody is troubled by ambiguity, I'm sure they would say so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If the witness feels that by answering by yes or no, the true sense of what was said would be lost, the witness is allowed to explain to us what he meant to say in answer to the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour. I couldn't possibly not, with respect, endorse that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mandic. In effect, I think what everybody is saying is if you feel the slightest nervousness that there's any doubt that you're accurately expressing your views, then please say so and we'll make sure that it's covered, and any confusion, as best we can, is cleared up. The last question I asked you, so let's just clear that up so there's no ambiguity. I'm suggesting to you that it was not the function of the Assembly to direct and interfere day by day with the executive functions of the government, and I'm inviting you to say whether you agree or disagree with that proposition.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I fully agree with you, Mr. Stewart. The Assembly could not, neither by virtue of its function nor was it possible for it to control day-to-day functioning of the government. The government was vested with executive power, and the military had military power.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Now, you were then asked by - this is at page 23, the same day, 1st of December - by His Honour Judge El Mahdi, immediately following on those questions and answers, His Honour said: "For instance, in this case, the government would report to the Assembly about its actions taken and activities. As far as you know - let me just find an appropriate term for this - can you tell us: Was the government informed about the goings-on on the ground? And I primarily refer to what was going on in the detention facilities, in other words, the destiny of the detainees, was it in some way told about it to the parliamentary deputies?" And you answered, Mr. Mandic: "The MPs," that's the deputies, "were very well-informed about the goings-on on the ground. They came from different areas, from different municipalities. They had firsthand information from the area where they resided in. As for the government and the level of the information that it had about the collection and detention facilities, they received information from the army and the police and they received as much information as there was, but the main sources of information were the army and the police respectively from the detention facilities that they held, and these were all the detention facilities that existed until the end of 1992, where prisoners were held." Now, Mr. Mandic, that in summary -- I wanted to read the full answer so there's no misunderstanding, but in summary, you're describing two sources of information there: The deputies, coming from the different parts of Republika Srpska, number 1; and number 2, the army and the police. Now, Mr. Mandic, if the deputies were fully informed about everything that was happening in their localities, and if at all times they reported what -- everything that they knew to their colleagues in the Assembly, and to the government, for that matter, then it would follow logically that everybody knew everything that was going on the whole time. So I'd like you to clarify for the Trial Chamber, Mr. Mandic: At the time that you became minister of justice, how effective was the channel of communication through the deputies from around Republika Srpska in conveying to the members of the Assembly and the government what was actually happening around Republika Srpska in relation to detention facilities?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me try to explain once again. When I talked about the deputies and the presidents of the municipalities, I was referring to the individuals who were members of War Presidencies or crisis committees. This means that they were informed of what was going on in their respective areas, where they worked, or rather, where they lived. It was very difficult for the Assembly to meet on a regular basis or to have sessions in a given area. The meetings were held at various places, because the movement was very difficult, the movement of the deputies from one part of Republika Srpska to the other. So when I talked about the deputies, when I talked about those people, I was referring to their responsibilities and the competences that they had in the areas where they lived and worked. As for the government, the government was briefed during the Assembly sessions by those people or through the military and the police. They were also informing the government of the goings-on in the entire territory of Republika Srpska. Very often, a commission would be established within the government and tasked with going out into the field to find out for themselves what was actually happening. Because there was a lot of misinformation as well, through various media, both Muslim and Serb media, but also through some international media as well. So this is why some of us in the government were rather confused when faced with all this information and misinformation at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: At the point, and it's a convenient point to take, Mr. Mandic, at the point that you became minister of justice, so 19th of May was your formal appointment, so let's say during that tail end of May. Let's take that as a period. How efficient and reliable was the flow of information into the government about what was happening in detention facilities in the different parts of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the first month or so, there was very poor -- there was a very poor flow of information in all the segments of government. Bosnia and Herzegovina was cut off in terms of roads, in terms of communication lines. It was difficult to get reliable information about what was going on in an area 30 kilometres away from Sarajevo, for instance.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honours, Ms. Cmeric believes that there was a reference in that answer which may have got lost, which included the word "chaos."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Again, if something is missing, we should not say what's missing, but ask -- give the context to the witness and then I don't think it's dramatic here, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I do recall Your Honour's injunction. Ms. Cmeric is exceptionally reliable on a single trigger word like that, and I wouldn't say it if I weren't completely confident in that word.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If it would not be on the basis of Ms. Cmeric's observations, I would have reacted far more strongly.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that is an appreciation of Ms. Cmeric.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: But thank, Your Honour. Ms. Cmeric is appreciated all around.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Cmeric, could you give us the words where -- nearby you think something was missing.

utterances.speaker: MS. CMERIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, it should be -- second sentence. It's in line -- it's page 51, line 22. So before words "Bosnia and Herzegovina" there's a sentence missing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, you told us that in the first month or so that there was a very poor flow of information in all the segments of the government. And then you said: "Bosnia and Herzegovina was cut off in terms of roads," et cetera. And it seems that part of what you said was missing. Could you tell us what you said, in addition to what I just put to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I said "chaos," I believe that this word adequately reflects the situation in Bosnia and Herzegovina in that first month.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for your clarification. Please proceed, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, you were asked some further questions by His Honour Judge El Mahdi, and I'm looking at page 27 of the transcript on the 1st of December. And in the middle of Judge El Mahdi's question, he said: "Leadership of Republika Srpska, when you say this, what do you exactly mean by it?" And you said: "The political means, the core leadership of the Serbian Democratic Party, that was the party bearing the power in Republika Srpska, and the state functionaries were the ones heading the state, the parliament, and certain regions." And His Honour said: "Can you be more precise and tell us their names?" And you said: "The personnel policy was run at the time by Dr. Karadzic, Dr. Biljana Plavsic, Dr. Nikola Koljevic, Mr. Momcilo Krajisnik, Rajko Dukic, and some other leaders of the regional boards of the Serbian Democratic Party whose names I cannot recall at present." On the 24th of November -- excuse me, Your Honour. It's a day that's lying on the floor down here. I'll just go and pick it up. On the 24th of November, at page 19 of the transcript, you had said: "Concerning the recruitment of personnel, and with the consent of Rajko Dukic and Karadzic, each municipality, the town and the region, proposed three members each from their own ethnic groups. The recruitment commission, Dukic and Karadzic, coordinated views with us and we had chosen the best people to be admitted into our ranks." I just want to clarify first with you, Mr. Mandic, so we don't get anything unfair here, that when you were talking about recruitment of personnel in that passage that I've just cited, you're talking, are you, in substance, about the same personnel policy as was being considered in answer to His Honour Judge El Mahdi's questions? We're talking about the same general issue of recruitment and appointment of personnel, are we?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe that this refers to the same periods of time. In 1991, when I was elected, appointed deputy, and when we were hiring people from the entire area of Bosnia and Herzegovina into the ministry, the main person in charge of personnel was Rajko Dukic, as the president of the Main Board of the SDS, and Dr. Radovan Karadzic, as president of the party. The main proposals of candidates from the regional and municipal levels throughout Bosnia and Herzegovina were the political leaders of SDS in these respective areas. I did not mention Mr. Krajisnik in this context because I never knew the man until mid-1991. And as far as personnel matters were concerned, he was never interested in the people working in the MUP until 1992, nor did he take any part in it. Therefore, for the high functionaries of the MUP, the approvals were given by Rajko Dukic and Dr. Karadzic, and for the lower-ranking officials, those would be the political leaders of the respective levels that would provide their approvals. Now, when I mentioned Mr. Krajisnik as part of the core political ^J state leadership, I was referring to 1992 and the nomination of ministers, general managers of the important public companies, chambers, and other organs that were object of election in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no further questions of Mr. Mandic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stewart. Mr. Tieger, is there any need to re-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I believe I have a brief re-examination, Your Honour. It won't take much time. I need to retrieve a document. I didn't anticipate we'd finish quite this quickly. But I won't be long.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps we would then first have a break until -- because usually we have a break at 5.30. We had a late start today. But we could have a break now if that -- if it would be --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I think that would be suitable, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll have a break until a quarter to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, are you ready to start, or Mr. Margetts, are you ready to start the re-examination of the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, yeah, but we have -- I think it was clear to the Court that we didn't anticipate the cross-examination would finish until sometime tomorrow, so we scrambled to get as many relevant documents as we could. I appreciate the fact that the Court wishes us to proceed, and under such circumstances, we would be prepared to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'd prefer to proceed, yes. Although it might have surprised you, it's not a surprise that -- I don't know whether you ever asked Mr. Stewart what he expected, when he would expect to finish his cross-examination. He might have had valuable information for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, the -- I didn't check with Mr. Stewart today, it is true. However, earlier estimates would have had us concluding tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Let's start, and let's see what happens. Mr. Mandic, Mr. Tieger will have one or more questions for you. Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, I think at one point during your cross-examination you made reference to, and I have the sequential numbers, which would be at page 8667, if that becomes relevant. But this is a prelude to my question. You made reference to the fact that actually, in terms of rank, you were the top official, top Bosnian Serb official, in the joint MUP. In fact, it wasn't the case, was it, Mr. Mandic, that you were the top-ranking Bosnian Serb official in the joint MUP?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The top-ranking Bosnian Serb in the joint MUP was the deputy minister, Vitomir Zepinic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, did Mr. Zepinic, along with Mr. Delimustafic, the minister of interior, have a well-known nickname by which they went? Are you familiar with the nicknames Boro and Ramiz?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And first of all, is it correct that Boro and Ramiz is a reference to two characters from World War II who fought together against fascism, one Serb, one Muslim, and who thereafter became effectively the symbols of -- or among the symbols of brotherhood and unity?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that there was a sports hall in Pristina called Boro and Ramiz. And you're probably right, Mr. Tieger, that these were men of different ethnicities who were friends, to say the least. If they were historical figures, then I don't know who they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, first of all, as a general matter, are you familiar with the use of their names as synonyms for brotherhood and unity?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, for the area of Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And were Mr. Zepinic and Mr. Delimustafic known as the Boro and Ramiz of the MUP or of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, this was more an object of derision rather than something serious, and I will explain to you what this is all about so that you and the Honourable Trial Chamber and the Defence can understand this. Mr. Delimustafic, as minister of the interior from the ranks of the Muslim people, was the richest man in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Conversely, Dr. Vitomir Zepinic was a person living in a bed-sitter in the neighbourhood of Otici [phoen] in Sarajevo. It was an apartment that had an area of 42 square metres. Now, you can imagine what their relationship and cooperation were like. If you need further explanation, I will provide them to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, is it -- was it the case that Mr. Zepinic was in favour of a joint MUP?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Initially, we were all in favour of a joint MUP, in the beginning of 1991, when we became functionaries in the joint MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: By the time that you, Mr. Kljajic, Mr. Zupljanin, and other high-ranking members of the joint MUP became proponents of a -- of an ethnically divided MUP, Mr. Zepinic continued to be in favour of a joint MUP; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Allow me to proceed with what I was going to say about Mr. Zepinic, Mr. Tieger. At the time the crisis in Bosnia-Herzegovina was in its incipient form in the end of 1991, Mr. Delimustafic - and this was something we established as a service - gave a Mazda 626 as a gift to Mr. Zepinic, and a locality near the Bosko Buha day care centre in Sarajevo. Those were business premises. And he lost credibility in the eyes of all the Serbs because he was, to us, a yes-man of Alija Delimustafic's, who, while being in the joint MUP and discharging his duties there, was also a trafficker in arms, that he obtained from Slovenia and other neighbouring countries. In the beginning of the war, the vehicle gave as a gift by Mr. Delimustafic was found in the neighbourhood of Kotorac, and Tomo Kovac's police torched it and blew up the locality at Lenjinova number 6 that had also been given as a gift by Delimustafic in Grbavica. We called them in a derisive manner as Boro and Ramiz because Delimustafic obtained arms for the Muslims and the other persons served for him as a cover-up while he was touring the area. On the 4th of April, he was asked to resign, to submit his resignation to the president of the Assembly of the Serbian People, Mr. Krajisnik, therefore, not to submit his resignation to the joint Assembly but to the Assembly of the Serbian People, to Mr. Krajisnik, because all the officials knew what sort of a man he was, and that was when he indeed resigned.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I may have missed it, Mr. Mandic, but it appears to me that not one word of your answer addressed my question, whether or not Mr. Zepinic was a proponent of the joint MUP at the time of the split of the MUP. And if you'd like, I can refer you to your previous --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You have to tell me whether he expressed himself in favour of the joint MUP at the official meetings, in his speeches, or whether he lobbied for it in some other way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, take the question as broad as possible. The question was whether he was in favour and whether you noticed this on private meetings, official meetings, whether -- whatever, tell us what you know about it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He was always supportive of the views of Mr. Delimustafic and did espouse the idea of a joint MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And didn't Mr. Zepinic and Mr. Delimustafic go to areas where there were national tensions and try to lower tensions, prior to the split of the MUP?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, you spoke during your earlier testimony, on page 78 of the December 7th transcript, about the arrangements that were made regarding the special units, and that was essentially, if I recall correctly, that there would be -- that a consensus would be required in order to activate the special units, in effect, giving each representative from each ethnic group a veto power over the deployment of the special units.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So, for example, if there was information that a predominantly Croat village was harbouring weapons, for whatever reasons, the Croat representative could prevent the deployment of the special unit, could prevent the special unit from acting, if he did not want those weapons discovered or confiscated?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But this was not abided by by the minister of MUP and the assistant minister for police, Avdo Hebib. In hierarchy, the Muslim leaders were the superior ones, and the agreement was not being implemented, whereas the Serbs and the Croats explicitly asked for all representatives of the three ethnicities to be in agreement over the issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And this agreement had the effect of effectively dividing the MUP, because if the minister of interior could not put the special unit into motion, then a unified MUP, essentially, didn't exist any more; would that be right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What mostly contributed to the division of the MUP was a transfer of the reserve police force to the active police force, and I'm referring to the ethnic Muslims. With the arrival of Mr. Srebrenkovic as assistant minister for personnel, every day hundreds of people were admitted on the force without informing other segments of the MUP prior to that, in order for such a possibility to arise for all the members of the different ethnicities.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I think you've already told us some of -- or already given us some of your reasons for why the split of the MUP eventually took place. I was asking you something different, and that was whether or not the division of the special units on an ethnic basis essentially equalled the division of a unified MUP.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. First, on the 31st of March, my dispatch was sent out, and only later on was the special unit split up. And this was agreed upon at a meeting in Krtelji. I believe it was on the 2nd or the 3rd of March. Therefore, after my dispatch, where all the three representatives of different ethnicities were present, and on that occasion, the special unit was split up in agreement, so to speak. There were 25 Serb members of the special unit who went to Rakovica, to a facility, in order to take the old facility of the unit at Vraca, that was a school, whereas in the new facility in Krtelji the rest of the special unit remained.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The number was, interpreters note, 35, not 25.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was led by Milenko Karisik, who was actually a deputy in the joint special unit. This remainder of the unit in Krtelji in the new base was run by Dragan Vikic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: After you felt you had reached an agreement with the special units concerning the ethnic division, did Mr. Zepinic meet with members of the special units?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that Mr. Zepinic was present at the meeting down there in Krtelji when this was agreed upon, but I don't believe that he met with the Serb part of the special unit after it had split up. I can't recall exactly who was present at the Krtelji meeting when they agreed upon the disbanding of the special unit, but I do know that all three ethnicities were represented.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, can the witness be presented again with Exhibit 419, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Registrar. Could the witness be given the B/C/S version, and could the English translation be put on the ELMO. Yes. When I say the B/C/S version, I do understand that it's only an English version because it's a -- it's an interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, Exhibit 419 is a transcript of a televised and taped interview you gave to Mr. Djogo, I believe in July or August of 1994. And that -- we actually have a copy of that, if it's necessary for you to take a look at the actual tape, or videotape of that interview.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you like to see it again, Mr. Mandic, or would you accept to work on the basis of a transcript?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the first time I see this, Your Honour. But there's no problem. I can answer the questions on the basis of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then, Mr. Tieger, put to the witness what you would like to put to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, let me direct your attention, then, to a portion of the interview which takes place at the time reference number 36:40, if you can find that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps you could -- is there a B/C/S version?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Have you found it?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, there's a reference, as we proceed, probably 15 to 20 lines into that passage of your comments, where you talk about the special meeting regarding -- with the members of the special units. You refer to the right of veto, meaning consensus, that is, if the special unit is sent somewhere, it can't do anything without the agreement of all three officials, of all three nationalities. You make reference to a comment by Mr. Pusina after the meeting that: "There's nowhere to go ..." Mandic has succeeded in dividing MUP. "There is no more unified MUP." And then you comment "because that was in fact the way it was. If Pusina Jusuf, as head of police, I mean that department can't put special unit in motion, meaning Delimustafic, that means unified MUP doesn't exist any more and somehow we carried it out." You then go on to note that: "Unfortunately, however, Vitomir Zepinic, meaning Alija Delimustafic, used all methods and lobbying people, called on our best special unit members, Miodrag Repija, Maric, and Jevtic, I believe, those are our best men, and promised them apartments, this and that, and it came to slight dilemma in the psychic [sic] of those people. You know, it is very hard to leave the system of one country." So, Mr. Mandic, does that refresh your recollection about Mr. Zepinic's efforts to disrupt the agreement regarding the special units and persuade Serbian members of the special units to remain in a unified MUP?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This precisely links up with what I was saying, that Mr. Zepinic had to follow Mr. Delimustafic's line blindly, and for some other reasons, advocate the idea of a joint unit. Now, when I was talking about the Pofalici events on Monday to the Defence and the engagement of the special units in the purely Serb areas, as a result, there was this -- there were -- difficulties there arose in a multi-ethnic MUP, and it was with this agreement that Mr. Delimustafic and Zepinic tried to have people on their side by buying them apartments, and this is -- these are Jevtic, Dusko Jevic [as interpreted] and some others. They were promised apartments to stay with them, in order to have this so-called joint MUP, only in its appearances, and I was against that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And Mr. Karisik reacted to this perceived threat to the division of the MUP; is that right, by informing you, Mr. Karadzic, and Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that he informed me about that, because Karisik was the second-highest official in the MUP. He was deputy to Predrag Vikic. And as the first one in the Serb cadre in MUP, he informed me and Mr. Krajisnik -- I don't know if also Mr. Karadzic was informed by him. I see that I mentioned it here, but I'm certain that he did inform Mr. Krajisnik and myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And then Mr. Krajisnik came up with the idea of -- or is it correct that Mr. Krajisnik came up with the idea of calling Zepinic to the Assembly, to Mr. Krajisnik's office?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so. I think it was Mico Stanisic's idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, can you tell us, then, why you credit calling Mr. Zepinic back to the Assembly to the "great wisdom of Krajisnik" when you spoke with Mr. Djogo on tape?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because at that point, I thought it good for Vitomir Zepinic to be isolated from Mr. Delimustafic, because we knew what their relationship was like. We knew what Mr. Delimustafic was doing behind this screen of Boro and Ramiz. And that's when I believe Mr. Zepinic submitted his resignation to Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, what was the question? Wasn't the question why you give credit to Mr. Krajisnik during that interview by saying that it was due to the great wisdom of Mr. Krajisnik that Mr. Zepinic was called to the Assembly? That was the question, why you give credit to Mr. Krajisnik, where you, in your previous answer, you said it was actually Mr. Stanisic's idea.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I must have been right in what I was saying. The idea for Mr. Krajisnik to invite Mr. Zepinic to the parliament was Mico Stanisic's, because Mico Stanisic and Vitomir Zepinic, who were both members of the ministerial council of the Serbian shadow government, were in serious conflict. Due to that, Mr. Krajisnik invited Vitomir Zepinic, and I came there, and some other Serb officials, and then Mr. Zepinic submitted his resignation to Mr. Krajisnik from the post of the deputy minister. This was in the premises of the joint Assembly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You give a lot of details that are not directly related to the question. Whose idea now was it to call Mr. Zepinic to the Assembly? Was it Mr. Krajisnik or was it Mr. Stanisic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe it was Mico Stanisic's idea, who suggested that Krajisnik do the practical part of it, to implement it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And what was the great wisdom, then, of Mr. Krajisnik to call him to the -- was that that he followed Mr. Stanisic's suggestion or ...?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And why exactly was that a demonstration of great wisdom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, because of the conflict between Stanisic and his deputy, Zepinic. Second, in our opinion, at the time, Zepinic was working on the breakup of this Serbian special unit, pursuant to an order of Delimustafic, by promising them apartments and various other privileges.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, in response to some questions by Mr. Stewart regarding the splitting of the MUP, and in particular, the comments in Ekstra magazine about your responsibility for splitting the MUP and thereby starting the conflict in Bosnia and Herzegovina, I believe you indicated that you wouldn't boast about something like that, and therefore, believe you had not said it. Would you boast about splitting the MUP and thereby dismantling an independent Bosnia and Herzegovina, and would you regard that as something different?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that moment, there was no independent Bosnia and Herzegovina. It came into existence on the 6th of April. And the message was sent on the 31st of March. So the Republic was still a part of the former Yugoslavia. It was called the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: But the splitting of the MUP, Mr. Mandic, was an attempt to forestall or prevent or undermine the establishment of an independent Bosnia and Herzegovina, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I only acted pursuant to the decisions of the Assembly of the Serbian People, in accordance with the constitution and the Law on the Internal Affairs. And when I was ordered, or rather, when the Sarajevo Agreement was signed, the agreement on the cantonal organisation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and based on the Cutileiro Plan, who was an negotiator for Bosnia and Herzegovina, it was then, pursuant to an order by Mico Stanisic, that I sent a memo to all the centres, because I, as chief of one of the departments, was the only one who could do that. This was all stated in the memo that I sent on the 31st of March. And just one thing, Mr. Tieger, that I would like to add. You did not show me the second part of this memo, of this letter, or rather, the second letter that I sent two days later, whereby I was informing them that in the future cantonal organisation of Bosnia-Herzegovina, there would be, as far as the MUP is concerned, a common educational system, and also the provision for common expenses and finances. This letter was sent a day or two days after the first one. My objective was to clarify the first letter, and it was done in the agreement with the representatives of the Serbian people and Mico Stanisic. This memo, this letter, can be found in the MUP in Sarajevo today. This was all in agreement with the Sarajevo Agreement, or the Cutileiro plan, which was initialled by Mr. Alija Izetbegovic, Radovan Karadzic, and Mate Boban.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So by your answer, Mr. Mandic, are you saying that the ethnic division of the MUP was not an attempt in any way to prevent or undermine the establishment of an independent Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it seems to me, to the extent I was aware of the political events in Bosnia and Herzegovina, that the leadership of the Serbian people, and the Serbian people themselves, wanted to arrange, wanted to organise the life in Bosnia and Herzegovina, because they were losing the common state they were living in, that they had been living in, the former Yugoslavia. And they believed that if Croats, Slovenes, and Macedonians had the right to self-determination, then the Serbian people within Bosnia-Herzegovina had the same right to self-determination and that cantons would be formed and that there would be a police force and the military formed alongside ethnic lines. This is all contained in the Sarajevo Agreement and the Cutileiro Plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I have to ask you again, Mr. Mandic, in that case: Does that, therefore, mean that the ethnic division of the MUP was an effort to prevent what the Bosnian Serb leadership feared as a result of the independence of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. Tieger says: "I have to ask you again." We question why he has to ask him again. This witness started off as Mr. Tieger's witness and there does come a point at which once a question has been asked, and it's been asked and developed and answered, there is a point at which it's been asked and counsel should move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Certainly has been asked, Your Honour, but I don't believe it's been answered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think the usual quote is question asked, question answered, but I think, as a matter of fact, Mr. Stewart, from the explanation the witness gives to his answer takes it that it's not a real answer to his question. So therefore, I would allow you to put that question again.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, you just told us about the political events, the reaction of the leadership of the Serbian people, their belief about what might happen if some peoples had the right to self-determination, and so on. My question is: Was the ethnic division of the MUP an attempt by the Bosnian Serb leadership to address concerns about the consequences of an independent Bosnia and Herzegovina, and thereby prevent a unified and independent Bosnia and Herzegovina from effectively coming into existence?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only give you my assumption, because I was not a member of the political or state leadership of Bosnian Serbs. I was a high-ranking official within the MUP, and I just carried out the tasks that I had been given. I don't know what the political leadership of Bosnian Serbs was afraid of. I was not aware of their concerns. It is quite probable that that was also one of their concerns, and it is probable that that was one of their fears as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: What, then, did you mean when you said to Mr. Djogo: "I went to Vraca with a 99 per cent chance to be killed as a terrorist." And forgive me. Let me direct your attention to the portion of the interview which takes place at 1:11:00. Just to repeat, you can find that portion, it's about the middle of that section: "I went to Vraca with a 99 per cent chance to be killed as a terrorist. As a man who, at that time, was responsible for dismantling an independent Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina." And the question was: What did you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So two years later, I was explaining to the editor of the Serb television, in light of my memories at the time, what the reasons were for the dismantling of the Serbian MUP and the special unit, and why it was decided at one point that one part of this joint special police force should go to Vraca. I was referring to the sovereign Bosnia and Herzegovina that was actually not sovereign at the time. Those were just my memories of the events two years later. This was just an unofficial conversation that I had with Mr. Djogo at the time when I visited Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters correction. After I had arrived from Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, moving on to another subject. You spoke, I believe earlier today, about the chain of command and -- regarding the military and who had the power to issue orders to the Bosnian Serb military forces. And I believe you said that the president of the Republic was at the very top of that chain of command and had the power to issue orders to the military and to the police.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, at the time, in fact, there wasn't a president of the Republic; there was a Presidency of the Republic. Isn't that right? That is, from May of 1992 until December of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that there was a Presidency, yes, and there was a president in the Presidency, Dr. Karadzic. Before him, it was Dr. Biljana Plavsic who had been the president. The Presidency existed for a relatively long period of time. I don't remember exactly how long. What I know for sure is that at the beginning of the war, it was Dr. Karadzic who was elected president of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and that there were two vice-presidents as well, Biljana Plavsic and Nikola Koljevic. They were members of the Presidency. They were the Presidency. That is how I remembered that the situation was, and please correct me if I'm wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So when you say "please correct me if I'm wrong," I take it that means that you were aware generally of the existence of a Presidency but haven't studied the constitutional documents relating to the establishment of the Presidency or the power of the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I haven't had the opportunity to study this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Is it also correct that you haven't had an opportunity to review or study minutes of the sessions of the Presidency?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Unless you're referring to the beginnings, the sessions of the government. But no, I never had an opportunity to review minutes of the sessions of the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And I presume you also haven't had a chance - it seemed incorporated in your answer - to study the provisions of law relating to the establishment of an Expanded Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And it would follow that you -- if you haven't seen minutes of the sessions of the Presidency, then you wouldn't have had an opportunity to see the listing of the members of that Presidency or Expanded Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Or to see how regularly or frequently the various members of that Presidency or Expanded Presidency attended the meetings.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And so when you spoke about Mr. Krajisnik's power to issue orders to the military or to the police, that was in light of the fact that you didn't know precisely who comprised the Presidency during that time, how regularly those members of the Presidency attended, and what decisions were made during the course of those Presidency meetings?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I spoke about this to Mr. Stewart, I referred to Mr. Krajisnik as the president of the Assembly and about his competences as such. I don't remember that his participation in the decision-making process was in any -- had any other form. This was not something that I was familiar with at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So your answer to Mr. Stewart was limited to what you understood about Mr. Krajisnik's powers as president of the Assembly only?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and also to what I knew from my contacts with Krajisnik about what he was doing, what his authority was. But exclusively, as far as his capacity as the president of the Assembly is concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I think Mr. Tieger should look at what I actually did ask, because I asked a follow-up question quite specifically after the question that I asked, which Mr. Tieger has just referred to.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, I don't have the -- of course, I obviously don't have the transcript and I don't have access to the LiveNote in front of me. If there's some way of identifying that particular passage, I'd be grateful. Or if the Court can give me a moment, we can scroll back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If you have two or three words, specific words, then it's easy to search for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It was towards the very end of my cross-examination today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Do you have one or two words, so that I could find it?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, it would follow on from --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Or the page number. That's fine as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It would certainly follow on from a reference to giving orders to the army, or something like that. I mean, it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll try to find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Formal. The word "formal" appeared. I think formal fogs or something. I'm just trying to remember, but I think I used the phrase "formal position." Certainly the word "formal."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Tieger, I find on page 46, line 12 -- no.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I suspect it's just above that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. I'm making a mistake because I'm on the wrong date. I apologise for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I suspect that the --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Page 46, line 7, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, let me attempt to deal with it, if I may, with the portion that appears to be relevant. If that's not the portion to which Mr. Stewart is referring, I believe he can let us know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, it was page 46, line 7.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then if you could find that, please, Mr. Tieger, and see whether ...

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, those line numbers do you not correspond.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me ask you -- the first of those two question was, "After all that, Mr. Mandic, my question --" I'm sorry, Your Honour, directed question directed to counsel?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That's right. I don't know what's happened about the lines. I never understand what goes on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll read the part I take it that ...

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Equality of arms, but inequality of lines between Prosecution and Defence. I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: After all that, Mr. Mandic, my question is a short, simple one, after a long introduction: "It's correct, isn't it, that Mr. Krajisnik, as president of the Assembly, had no authority over the army?" The answer is yes. And the next question is: "And he had no other position which gave him authority over the army?" The answer was: "No, he didn't." Those are the lines you're referring to, I take it, Mr. -- Although without the word "formal."

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. I'd imagined that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, may I -- it seems that you're struggling through. Would you have any further questions? Because we would then stop now and I would ask you then to continue tomorrow. But if it's just a matter of one or two questions, I would like to ask you to finish now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, it depends, obviously, these even seemingly simple questions drag on, but I will make an effort to complete it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. How much time would you still need for that? Because I have already a bad reputation with the interpreters and the technicians.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, I've got two documents I want to focus on, Your Honour. I think it takes -- I would estimate five and no more than ten. But I know the Court has seen us try to move quickly through it and it doesn't always happen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, experience teaches us that what seems to be five or ten minutes easily will be 15 to 17 minutes, so therefore, we'd rather continue tomorrow. We might have decided otherwise if there would not have been several procedural issues the Chamber would like to deal with anyhow tomorrow in the afternoon. At the same time, the Chamber still hopes that you would keep to your time-limits. Your indication of time, as you have given today. I don't know whether there are any arrangements made already for Mr. Mandic. Mr. Mandic, are you aware of how your travelling is scheduled? Are you supposed to leave tomorrow in the afternoon or Saturday morning? What's the -- what are the plans? I do take it from your nodding that it will not be -- your departure has not been scheduled on Friday. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have been informed that the Defence would be questioning me for three days, so I was supposed to travel back on Saturday. This is a new development, the fact that the Defence has finished.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then, under those circumstances, where continuing tomorrow does not change any scheduled arrangements, the Chamber would prefer to continue tomorrow. As I said before to the parties, that the Chamber would need another 45 minutes for procedural issues. That might even be a bit more, because the Chamber would like to deliver a decision also on all the 92 bis pending motions at this moment, which is, apart from that, the parties will be provided with the exhibit list tomorrow so that we can quickly go through that in respect of Mr. Mandic, once he has concluded his testimony. Mr. Mandic, I again have to ask you to come back, although it will be for a relatively short moment, tomorrow in the afternoon, quarter past 2.00, if I'm well-informed, in this same courtroom. We adjourn until tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 10th day of December 2004, at 2.15 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 7.02 p.m.,
